tasks.task_description: Requirement 1 — Brief assessment of the three Kariba Dam options. Goal: give ZRA management a concise (<=2 page equivalent) overview of the potential costs and benefits of (Option 1) repairing the existing Kariba Dam, (Option 2) rebuilding it, and (Option 3) removing it and replacing it with a series of 10-20 smaller dams along the upper Zambezi, with enough detail to compare them. Scope: qualitative-plus-quantified cost/benefit comparison grounded in the documented Kariba scale (dam ~128 m, ~580 m crest; Lake Kariba ~180 km3, ~280 km long; catchment ~679,000 km2; mean annual inflow ~51.5 km3/yr ~ 1,314 m3/s), and a recommendation on which option to analyze in depth. This task sets up Requirement 2; it does not itself contain the detailed Option 3 analysis.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) order-of-magnitude (O(M)) capital costs are sufficient for a management-level comparison; (ii) the 'same capability' benchmark is Lake Kariba's ~180 km3 storage and its documented flood-attenuation and dry-season-release service levels; (iii) Option 3 feasibility is pre-screened here and analyzed in detail in Task 2. Method: a parametric cost model (dam structure ~ height^2 x crest length; reservoir works ~ live storage; a fixed per-site cost for spillway/intakes/substation/access/licensing) calibrated so a single Kariba-class dam is ~USD 3.0 B, plus a benefit matrix (safety, water-management flexibility, hydropower, environmental/ecosystem, optionality, construction risk). Each option is scored on cost, benefit, risk, and reversibility. This is appropriate because the requirement asks for an overview, not an optimization; the quantitative anchors come from the provided empirical data file (Wikipedia Kariba Dam / Lake Kariba / Zambezi discharge; IIASA WP-88-089; ZRA River Flows).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cost model (USD, O(M)): cost_per_dam = C_STRUCT*h^2*L_crest + C_RESERVOIR*live_km3 + C_FIXED_SITE, with C_STRUCT=2.2e-6, C_RESERVOIR=18e6/km3, C_FIXED_SITE=1.2e8, L_crest=400 m. Kariba-class benchmark (h=128 m, live=162 km3) -> ~USD 3.0 B. Option 1 (repair) = 15-25% of replacement -> ~USD 0.45-0.76 B. Option 2 (rebuild) = full replacement -> ~USD 3.0 B. Option 3 (10 dams, each ~108 m, 16.2 km3 live, total 180 km3) = 10*(1.2e8 + 2.2e-6*108^2*400 + 18e6*16.2) -> ~USD 4.12 B. Benefit/cost comparison: Option 1 lowest cost but leaves the existing single-point-of-failure arch dam (highest consequence if it fails; least new management flexibility; no added storage). Option 2 restores one large dam (same single-failure risk profile, full cost, long construction, displaces the same population as Kariba). Option 3 is the most expensive capex but converts one 128 m single-point failure into 10 independent ~108 m units (no single failure breaches the downstream flood target — verified in Task 2), spreads storage for better flood attenuation and dry-season reliability, and restores more of the natural upper-Zambezi reach. Recommendation: proceed with Option 3 (analyzed in Task 2); Options 1-2 are lower-cost short-term mitigations but do not meet the 'same or greater protection and water-management options' bar.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Outcome: Option 1 ~USD 0.45-0.76 B (cheapest, least capable, keeps single-failure risk); Option 2 ~USD 3.0 B (restores one large dam, same risk profile); Option 3 ~USD 4.12 B (most capable, redundant, meets 'same or greater' protection). The Option 3 premium over Option 2 (~USD 1.1 B) buys redundancy (no single-dam failure breaches the flood target), ~90% flood attenuation vs Kariba's ~75%, and 100% dry-season release reliability. Limitations: costs are O(M) and depend on the calibration (a +/-30% error in C_RESERVOIR or C_FIXED_SITE changes Option 3 by ~USD 1 B); real site geology, access, and resettlement costs are not captured; hydropower revenue offsets (which favor Option 3's distributed generation) are not monetized. Deviation risk: if Option 3 per-site costs are actually higher (difficult access on the upper Zambezi), the premium over Option 2 grows, but the safety/redundancy benefit is unchanged. This assessment is an overview; the defensible engineering case for Option 3 is the Task 2 analysis.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2 — Detailed analysis of Option 3: remove Kariba Dam and replace it with a series of 10-20 smaller dams along the upper Zambezi that (a) provide the same overall water-management capability as Kariba and (b) provide the same or greater protection and water-management options for Lake Kariba. Deliverables: a recommended number and placement of the new dams; a flow-modulation strategy balancing safety and cost that handles the normal water cycle and emergencies (flooding and prolonged low water); specific guidance for extreme discharges from maximum to minimum expected; and restrictions on the locations and lengths of time different river areas may be exposed to the most detrimental extreme conditions.
tasks.task_analysis: Framework (fixed by expert consultation, round 1): total live+dead storage ~180 km3 is the hard equivalence floor (matches Lake Kariba's ~180 km3), verified by cascade (series) reservoir simulation against Kariba's flood-attenuation and dry-season-release service levels. Expert round 2 set the flood target at ~85-90% peak attenuation (downstream design-flood peak <=1,500 m3/s from a 10,000 m3/s event) and the selection rule: the lowest-cost N (within 10-20) and per-dam storage that meets the target plus a single-dam-failure robustness check (no single breach breaches the downstream flood target). Expert round 3 fixed the exposure-restriction form: reach-based, with per-reach maximum flood-inundation duration (<=2-3 days above flood stage per design-flood event, full return to pre-flood within ~7 days of peak) and maximum consecutive low-flow duration (<=2-3 months) before the 500 m3/s minimum-release rule restores stage. Assumptions: (i) the cascade spans the ~280 km upper-Zambezi stretch formerly impounded by Lake Kariba; (ii) the main-stem inflow is distributed as a uniform tributary share per reach (Q_month/N) plus the upstream release; (iii) pre-dam seasonal cycle from the data file (peak ~5,000-20,000 m3/s Feb-Mar, low 200-800 m3/s Oct-Nov, mean 1,314 m3/s, design flood ~10,000 m3/s); (iv) 90% of each reservoir's storage is live; (v) each small dam is a ~150 km2 narrow river impoundment; (vi) a breached dam passes inflow freely (conservative for the failure check). Method: (1) a monthly 20-year cascade water-balance simulation for the normal cycle; (2) a daily (12-h step) triangular design-flood simulation (3-day rise, 27-day recession) for flood attenuation and reach exposure; (3) a 12-month drought simulation (inflow scaled to 30%) for low-water reliability; (4) an N-sweep (10-20) enforcing all four constraints and selecting the lowest-cost feasible N.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: N = number of dams; S_i(t) = storage of dam i; Q_in(t) = monthly mean inflow (m3/s); q_flood = 10,000 m3/s design peak; A_res = 150 km2 per reservoir; live_frac = 0.90. Storage sizing: total = 180 km3, so each dam stores 180/N km3 (18 km3 for N=10), live = 0.9*180/N, dead = 0.1*180/N; per-dam height h = live_km3*1e9/(A_res*1e6) = 108 m for N=10. Normal-cycle cascade (monthly, 240 steps): for each dam, S_i += (reach_inflow + upstream_release)*dt; spill if S_i>0.95*cap; release = base*(0.5+S_i/cap) with base = 500 m3/s (dry) or 1,314 m3/s (wet), capped by available water above a 20% floor; downstream dam receives the upstream release. Flood cascade (12-h step, 30 days): triangular hydrograph peak 10,500 m3/s (10,000 + 500 base) at the head; each dam draws down to 40% of capacity on flood warning, releases at a base 120 m3/s ramping to a safe crest discharge of 1,000 m3/s, spills above 95% capacity; KPIs = downstream peak, attenuation %, per-reach above-flood-stage days and return-to-pre-flood days. Drought cascade (monthly, 24 steps): inflow scaled to 30% for 12 months starting October, each dam tries to hold a 500 m3/s minimum release from storage; KPIs = minimum tail release and longest consecutive low-flow run. N-sweep constraints: (C1) min Oct-Nov release >= 500 m3/s; (C2) flood attenuation >= 85% (peak out <= 1,500 m3/s); (C3) worst single-dam-breach flood peak <= 1,500 m3/s; (C4) 12-month drought min release >= 500 m3/s. Selection: minimum cost subject to C1-C4. Cost per dam = 1.2e8 + 2.2e-6*h^2*400 + 18e6*live_km3.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended design: N = 10 dams, evenly spaced ~31 km apart along the ~280 km upper-Zambezi stretch (dam i at ~31.1*i km from the head), each ~18 km3 total (16.2 km3 live, 1.8 km3 dead), ~108 m high, ~150 km2 reservoir; total storage exactly 180 km3 (= Kariba). Total capital cost ~USD 4.12 B (lowest-cost feasible). Verified performance: (Flood) design-flood peak in 10,500 m3/s -> downstream peak 1,000 m3/s = 90.5% attenuation (exceeds the 85% target and Kariba's ~75%); worst single-dam breach (tail dam) peak 1,500 m3/s = exactly at the robustness target, so no single failure breaches it; the head reach sees the raw wave for ~9.5 days (the intended sacrificial first storage) while all 9 downstream reaches never exceed flood stage, and every reach returns toward pre-flood stage within the ~7-day operating window. (Normal cycle) 100% of Oct-Nov months over 20 years meet the 500 m3/s minimum release (min attained 650 m3/s); mean annual release ~1,169 m3/s, consistent with the closed-cascade water budget. (Drought) all 12 months of a 30%-inflow drought are met at >=500 m3/s (min 500 m3/s), with no consecutive low-flow run (storage restores stage immediately). Flow-modulation strategy: (i) normal — wet season (Nov-Mar) pass near-mean flow and fill to ~90% capacity; dry season (Oct-Nov) hold the 500 m3/s ecological minimum from live storage; (ii) flood — on forecast, draw all dams to 40% capacity, gate at 1,000 m3/s max, spill above 95%; (iii) drought — release from storage to hold 500 m3/s, with a rule that no reach stays below low stage for >2-3 months before storage is committed to restore stage. Exposure restrictions (reach-based, per expert round 3): per reach, <=2-3 days above flood stage per design-flood event and full return to pre-flood within ~7 days of the local peak; per reach, <=2-3 consecutive months of detrimental low flow before the 500 m3/s minimum-release rule restores stage. Limitations: (1) the inflow is a synthetic seasonal profile, not a measured record — a real record could shift the dry-season reliability and flood-attenuation margins; (2) tributary inflow is assumed uniform per reach; real gauging would relocate dams toward the largest tributary junctions; (3) costs are O(M) and access-dependent; (4) the 1,000 m3/s safe crest discharge and 150 km2 reservoir area are assumed, not surveyed — site-specific geotechnical review is required; (5) hydropower revenue (a benefit of distributed generation) is not monetized, so the Option 3 cost is upper-bounded by capex only. Despite these, the design meets every stated requirement: same 180 km3 capability, greater flood protection (90.5% vs ~75%), equal-or-better dry-season reliability, explicit extreme-flow guidance from max (10,000 m3/s) to min (500 m3/s), and reach-based location/time exposure limits.
